strengths: Long-RVOS addresses a meaningful gap in referring video object segmentation. Its 2,193 videos average 60.3 seconds, with 2.1M masks and 24,689 descriptions (Table 1), substantially extending the temporal coverage of the compared benchmarks. Multiple objects and explicit selection for interrupted visibility make it a useful setting for studying disappearance, reappearance, and distractors.

The annotation process involves substantial human oversight: expert verification of descriptions and iterative checking and correction of SAM2-generated masks. Explicit static, dynamic, and hybrid description categories enable more informative evaluation than a single aggregate score.

Benchmarking six recent methods provides a useful empirical reference. The SAM2 ground-truth-prompt experiment also demonstrates substantial tracking difficulty: approximately 53–54 J&F on Long-RVOS versus 77–81 on MeViS (Table 3a).

ReferMo offers a practical baseline combining compressed motion information, keyframe reasoning, and mask propagation. It improves overall J&F from ReferDINO’s 48.7 to 51.3 and vIoU from 41.2 to 42.6, with reported throughput increasing from 46.4 to 52.5 FPS. Motion ablation supports a contribution from motion features: full-video J&F rises from 49.7 to 51.3.

Overall, the substantial benchmark contribution and useful baseline favor acceptance. Its value does not depend on strong architectural novelty, although the metric interpretation and experimental attribution need qualification.
weaknesses: The claimed temporal-consistency evaluation is narrower than presented. tIoU measures nonempty-mask presence and cannot distinguish correct tracking from segmenting an unrelated object during the same frames. Equation (2) averages frame IoUs over the temporal union; it is not the stated volumetric intersection-over-union, which would aggregate pixel intersection and union counts. These metrics also do not explicitly measure temporal ordering or identity continuity. An always-present prediction baseline would help interpret the tightly clustered tIoU results around 68–72.

The experiments do not fully isolate ReferMo’s architectural benefits. The main comparison changes motion processing, frame selection, and SAM2 propagation simultaneously. Keyframe gains over ReferDINO are only 0.5 J&F, and there is no controlled ReferDINO-plus-equivalent-SAM2-propagation comparison or ablation of global interaction. The motion ablation is useful, but stronger claims about the local-to-global design and long-term reasoning remain under-supported.

Important benchmark validation details are missing. The manuscript reports split sizes but does not explain source-video or recording-level separation across the heterogeneous source datasets. It also lacks quantitative audits of residual mask errors and expression ambiguity, and statistics on disappearance frequency, absence duration, and shot changes. These omissions limit assessment of the benchmark’s reliability and the prevalence of its defining challenges; they do not establish that leakage or annotation errors occurred.

Some interpretations exceed the evidence. Lower SAM2 tracking scores across two different datasets demonstrate greater difficulty but do not isolate video length from differences in content and annotation. Similarly, poor performance of SAM2-based RVOS methods does not establish that their previous gains primarily came from tracking rather than language understanding. Duration-controlled comparisons and evaluations by disappearance or shot-change difficulty would make these conclusions more convincing. ReferMo also does not improve temporal presence accuracy: its tIoU is 71.2 versus ReferDINO’s 71.7.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Motion extraction details are deferred to supplementary material that is not included; annotation/evaluation frame sampling, model-specific baseline adaptations, and empty-mask decision rules are insufficiently specified. The reported FPS excludes video loading, but whether motion extraction is included is unclear. These details matter for reproducing both the accuracy and efficiency claims.

strengths: Long-RVOS addresses a meaningful gap in referring video object segmentation. Its 2,193 videos average 60.3 seconds, substantially exceeding the durations of the compared benchmarks, and provide 24,689 descriptions and 2.1 million masks. This is a useful benchmark contribution independently of the baseline method’s novelty.

The annotation process is substantive: descriptions undergo expert validation, and SAM2-generated masks undergo an iterative human checking and correction process, including removal of masks in object-absent frames. Explicit static, dynamic, and hybrid descriptions enable more informative evaluation than a single aggregate score.

The experiments cover six recent methods, with separate results by description type. SAM2’s first-frame ground-truth-prompt results fall from approximately 77–81 J&F on MeViS to 53–55 on Long-RVOS, providing concrete evidence that the collected videos pose substantial tracking challenges.

ReferMo provides a practical baseline using compressed-video motion vectors, keyframe reasoning, and mask propagation. It improves overall J&F from ReferDINO’s 48.7 to 51.3 and vIoU from 41.2 to 42.6. The motion ablation supports a contribution from motion information: removing it reduces overall J&F to 49.7.

Overall, the substantial dataset, documented annotation effort, and useful baseline comparisons favor acceptance. The reservations primarily limit the interpretation and reproducibility of particular claims rather than invalidate the central benchmark contribution.
weaknesses: The metric claims need substantive qualification. Equation (2) averages per-frame IoUs over the temporal union; it is not the stated spatiotemporal volume IoU, which would aggregate pixel intersections and unions before division. Moreover, tIoU measures presence detection, not identity preservation or temporal smoothness: even an incorrectly located nonempty mask counts as a positive presence prediction. These metrics are useful complements, but do not establish temporal consistency as broadly claimed.

The benchmark lacks quantitative characterization of its defining challenges. The paper does not report distributions of disappearance durations, reappearance events, occlusions, or shot changes, nor performance stratified by these factors or video length. The MeViS comparison establishes a dataset difficulty difference but does not isolate video duration from changes in content and object composition.

The method comparisons only partially isolate the source of improvement. ReferMo adds SAM2 propagation to a ReferDINO-derived architecture, while ReferDINO is evaluated without SAM2. The motion ablation is informative, but a matched ReferDINO-plus-propagation control and an ablation of global interaction would better establish the individual contributions. ReferMo also decreases tIoU from 71.7 to 71.2, so its gains do not extend to the proposed temporal metric.

Some causal interpretations exceed the evidence. Poorer results for SAM2-based competitors do not establish that their previous gains primarily came from segmentation rather than language understanding; the oracle experiment itself demonstrates substantial tracking difficulty. Similarly, differences between description types do not cleanly establish static-cue bias because descriptions can be skipped when a type cannot uniquely identify an object, potentially producing different evaluation populations.

Reproducibility and dataset reliability are incompletely documented. The manuscript gives split sizes but does not explain source-video grouping or duplicate checks across the constituent datasets, specify annotation sampling cadence clearly, or quantify residual mask and description errors. Baseline-specific training and long-video inference settings are also sparse. These are meaningful gaps for a benchmark, although the reported human validation process provides some reassurance.

strengths: Long-RVOS makes a substantial benchmark contribution to language-guided video segmentation: 2,193 videos averaging 60.3 seconds, 6,703 objects, 24,689 expressions, and 2.1 million masks. Its emphasis on distractors, disappearance, and reappearance addresses a meaningful gap in existing short-video benchmarks.

The annotation process includes credible quality controls: expert verification of referring expressions and iterative human checking and correction of SAM2-generated masks, including removal of masks on object-absent frames. The approximately balanced static, dynamic, and hybrid expression categories support useful diagnostic evaluation.

The six-method benchmark provides meaningful evidence of difficulty. SAM2 with ground-truth initial prompts achieves only 52.8–54.5 J&F on Long-RVOS, compared with 77.3–80.6 on MeViS, demonstrating a substantial tracking challenge even without language-based initialization.

ReferMo offers a practical baseline combining compressed motion information, keyframe grounding, and mask propagation. Table 2 reports improvements over ReferDINO from 48.7 to 51.3 J&F and from 41.2 to 42.6 vIoU, with higher reported throughput. Removing motion reduces full-video J&F from 51.3 to 49.7, providing direct support for its usefulness.

Overall, the dataset's scale, annotation effort, and diagnostic value provide a stronger case for acceptance than the methodological and reporting limitations provide against it. The contribution does not depend on treating ReferMo as a fundamentally new architecture.
weaknesses: The metric interpretation needs correction. Equation (2) averages framewise IoU over the union of predicted and ground-truth presence frames; it is not volumetric intersection divided by volumetric union, which weights frames by mask-union area. Moreover, tIoU measures presence agreement rather than identity or motion consistency: predicting any nonempty mask in every frame yields the target's visibility fraction. An always-present baseline and explicit empty-mask conventions are needed to interpret the tightly clustered tIoU results.

The experiments only partially isolate ReferMo's advantages. Relative to ReferDINO, the system changes temporal sampling, motion encoding, and SAM2 propagation. The motion ablation is useful, but there is no matched ReferDINO-plus-SAM2 comparison or ablation of global interaction. Thus, the evidence supports the complete system and motion features more strongly than the claimed contribution of long-term reasoning. ReferMo also decreases tIoU from 71.7 to 71.2.

Dataset reliability and split independence are incompletely documented. The manuscript gives split sizes but does not explain grouping by original source video, recording, or scene, or duplicate handling across its multiple sources. It also lacks quantitative annotation audits and distributions of disappearance intervals, shot changes, and occlusions. These omissions limit assessment of the benchmark's central long-term properties; they do not establish that leakage or annotation errors occurred.

Some causal conclusions exceed the evidence. Lower performance of SAM2-based referring methods does not establish that their previous gains primarily came from segmentation rather than language understanding. Likewise, the cross-dataset oracle comparison establishes greater difficulty but does not isolate duration from differences in content and visibility. Controlled temporal truncation or challenge-specific analyses would support these interpretations more directly.

Reproducibility is only partial in the supplied manuscript. Motion extraction is deferred to supplementary material that is not included, baseline-specific training and long-video inference configurations are sparse, and the Project Page field is empty. Frame-sampling and mask-thresholding details are especially relevant to reproducing the temporal metrics. Separately, minor statistical inconsistencies—such as 6,703 objects across 2,193 videos versus the stated average of 3.4 objects per video—need clarification.

strengths: Long-RVOS addresses a meaningful gap in referring video object segmentation: 2,193 videos averaging 60.3 seconds, with 2.1 million masks and 24,689 descriptions. Its scale and substantially longer sequences provide a useful contribution independently of the proposed model.

Dataset construction includes explicit object-selection criteria, expert validation of descriptions, and iterative checking and correction of SAM2-generated masks. Static, dynamic, and hybrid descriptions support more informative evaluation than a single aggregate score.

The evidence supports increased difficulty: Table 8 reports substantially more full occlusion, out-of-view events, and long-term reappearance than MeViS. First-frame ground-truth mask prompting also yields much lower SAM2 performance on Long-RVOS than MeViS (55.6 versus 80.6 J&F on the reported test/validation comparisons).

ReferMo provides a practical baseline with measurable benefits. It improves test J&F from ReferDINO's 48.4 to 52.9 and vIoU from 43.9 to 45.2, while reporting 52.5 FPS. Validation results, propagation alternatives, and motion-fusion ablations provide additional support.

Overall, the substantial benchmark contribution and supported segmentation improvements favor acceptance, despite reservations about metric interpretation, experimental attribution, and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The metric claims need correction. Equation 2 averages per-frame IoUs over the temporal union; it is not the stated spatiotemporal volume IoU, which would aggregate pixel intersections and unions before division. Also, tIoU measures presence agreement rather than identity or trajectory consistency: predicting any nonempty mask on the correct frames can score perfectly. These metrics are useful, but their interpretation and claimed novelty are overstated.

Improved temporal presence prediction is not convincingly demonstrated. Test tIoU changes only from 73.5 to 73.6 relative to ReferDINO, and validation tIoU decreases from 74.7 to 74.3. The claim of consistent improvements across all types and metrics is therefore incorrect. An always-present baseline and explicit empty-mask decision rules would help interpret these results.

The ablations do not fully isolate the source of the overall gain. Table 4b evaluates decomposition and motion only on keyframes, whereas the headline comparison includes SAM2 propagation. A matched ReferDINO-keyframe-plus-SAM2 baseline evaluated on all frames is missing. Global interaction contributes only a small reported gain, limiting evidence for the stronger long-term reasoning claims.

Benchmark reliability and reproducibility remain incompletely documented. The manuscript does not specify source-video grouping or duplicate checks across splits, annotation sampling cadence, quantitative mask-quality auditing, or detailed baseline training schedules. These omissions matter for a benchmark assembled from overlapping video collections and evaluated using model-assisted annotations.

Training every method solely on Long-RVOS provides a useful controlled comparison, but does not establish that prior SAM2-based methods succeed mainly through tracking rather than language understanding. The manuscript itself notes that MLLM-based methods depend on larger training corpora; their poor results under this protocol cannot cleanly establish the proposed causal explanation.

Some readily correctable reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in the ablation interpretation: Table 5 lists J=49.8 and F=50.4 but J&F=49.8, and Figure 5 reports 3.4 objects per video despite the totals implying approximately 3.1. These are secondary to the substantive concerns above.

strengths: Long-RVOS addresses a meaningful benchmark gap: 2,193 videos averaging 60.3 seconds, 6,703 objects, 24,689 descriptions, and 2.1 million masks substantially extend the temporal scope of existing RVOS datasets. This resource contribution provides the main justification for weak acceptance.

Dataset construction includes substantial human oversight: expert validation of descriptions and iterative inspection and correction of SAM2-generated masks. Explicit static, dynamic, and hybrid descriptions enable useful diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate segmentation accuracy.

The increased difficulty is supported by evidence. Table 8 reports substantially more full occlusion, out-of-view events, and long-term reappearance than MeViS. Ground-truth-prompted SAM2 also performs markedly worse on Long-RVOS than on MeViS (Table 4a), demonstrating challenges beyond language grounding alone.

ReferMo provides a practical baseline with consistent segmentation gains. It improves test J&F from ReferDINO’s 48.4 to 52.9 and validation J&F from 49.6 to 53.7, while reporting 52.5 versus 46.4 FPS. Improvements extend across description types and occlusion brackets.

The experiments include seven competing methods, component ablations, alternative propagation models, and supplementary analyses of description length and event complexity. These provide useful initial evidence for the benchmark and baseline.
weaknesses: The temporal-metric claims exceed what the definitions establish. Equation 2 averages framewise IoU over the union of foreground-present frames; it is not a literal spatiotemporal volume IoU, which would aggregate pixel intersections and unions before division. Both proposed metrics lack an explicit measure of ordering, fragmentation, or identity continuity. They provide useful complementary evaluation, but their novelty and interpretation as temporal consistency measures are overstated.

ReferMo does not convincingly improve presence/absence prediction. Test tIoU changes only from 73.5 to 73.6 relative to ReferDINO, and validation tIoU decreases from 74.7 to 74.3. The statement that it improves across all types and metrics is therefore incorrect. An always-present baseline would help establish whether the reported tIoU scores reflect meaningful absence detection.

The attribution of gains to long-term reasoning remains incomplete. Table 4b supports a 1.1-point keyframe gain from motion, but does not report full-sequence results for each component under identical propagation. A matched ReferDINO-plus-SAM2 comparison would clarify the source of the overall improvement. Global interaction adds only 0.4 points with motion in Table 5, without uncertainty estimates. The architecture largely combines existing components, so its methodological originality is modest.

Benchmark reproducibility and quality assurance are incompletely documented. The manuscript gives split sizes but not the source-aware splitting or duplicate-control procedure, annotation sampling cadence, or quantitative mask/text quality audit. Baseline-specific training settings, empty-mask prediction rules, and evaluation aggregation details are also insufficiently specified. These omissions matter for a benchmark centered on disappearance and reappearance.

Some broader conclusions are insufficiently controlled. Training all methods only on Long-RVOS establishes performance under that regime, but does not establish that SAM2-based methods’ previous successes primarily reflect tracking rather than language understanding. Similarly, description-type comparisons involve potentially different object subsets because annotation types can be skipped, and event complexity is inferred from textual keywords. These analyses are informative but do not isolate the claimed capabilities.

There are correctable numerical inconsistencies: Table 5 lists J=49.8 and F=50.4 but J&F=49.8 rather than 50.1, affecting the claimed global-interaction gain; Figure 5 reports 3.4 objects per video, whereas the stated totals imply approximately 3.06. These require clarification but do not outweigh the dataset contribution.

strengths: Long-RVOS makes a valuable benchmark contribution: 2,193 videos averaging 60.3 seconds, 6,703 objects, 2.1M masks, and 24,689 descriptions substantially extend the temporal scope of existing RVOS evaluation. This contribution provides the main basis for weak acceptance.

The annotation process is thoughtfully designed, with expert verification of distinguishing descriptions and iterative checking and correction of SAM2-generated masks. Balanced static, dynamic, and hybrid descriptions support useful diagnostic evaluation.

The long-video challenges are supported by evidence. Table 8 reports substantially more full occlusion, out-of-view events, and long-term reappearance than MeViS; the ground-truth-prompt SAM2 experiments independently demonstrate tracking difficulty.

ReferMo is a useful, technically plausible baseline combining compressed motion information, keyframe reasoning, and mask propagation. It improves test J&F from ReferDINO's 48.4 to 52.9 while reporting higher throughput, with similar gains on validation.

Experiments cover seven recent methods, alternative mask propagators, motion-fusion ablations, and performance across occlusion levels and description complexity. These analyses provide meaningful support beyond a single aggregate benchmark result.
weaknesses: The temporal-metric claims need qualification. Equation 2 averages frame IoUs over the union of visible timestamps; it is not a true spatiotemporal volume IoU, which would aggregate pixel intersections and unions before division. Moreover, tIoU measures presence detection rather than identity continuity or temporal smoothness. An always-present baseline would help interpret its relatively high values.

The claim of consistent improvement across all metrics is unsupported. Test tIoU changes only from 73.5 to 73.6 relative to ReferDINO, while validation tIoU decreases from 74.7 to 74.3. The strongest evidence is for spatial segmentation improvement, with smaller vIoU gains, rather than improved temporal presence prediction.

Attribution to long-term reasoning remains incomplete. Table 4b supports a 1.1-point keyframe gain from motion, but Table 5 shows only a 0.4-point benefit from global interaction when motion is enabled. A matched ReferDINO-plus-SAM2 propagation control is absent, limiting separation of architectural gains from propagation benefits.

Benchmark reliability and reproducibility are incompletely documented. The manuscript gives split sizes but does not explain source-video or recording-level separation and duplicate checks across its multiple sources. It also lacks quantitative mask-quality audits, agreement measurements for description validation, and detailed baseline training configurations. These omissions leave uncertainty without establishing that leakage or annotation errors actually occurred.

Training every method only on Long-RVOS is a useful controlled setting, but it does not establish the best achievable performance of methods designed for broader training. The resulting scores do not isolate the paper's proposed explanation that prior SAM2-based improvements primarily reflect tracking rather than language understanding.

There are correctable numerical inconsistencies: Table 5 reports J&F of 49.8 for J=49.8 and F=50.4, whose average is 50.1, undermining the stated 0.2-point global-interaction gain. Figure 5's mean of 3.4 objects per video also does not match 6,703 objects across 2,193 videos, approximately 3.06.
